content: Polo-like kinase 1 (PLK1), also referred to as serine/threonine-protein kinase PLK1 or STPK13, is an enzyme encoded by the PLK1 gene in humans. It plays a critical role in cell cycle regulation and mitotic progression. PLK1 is composed of 603 amino acids and has a molecular weight of 66 kDa. Structurally, it contains a kinase domain at the N-terminus and two conserved polo-box regions, each consisting of 30 amino acids, at the C-terminus. These polo-box regions are essential for regulating kinase activity, contributing to both auto-inhibition and subcellular localization. During interphase, PLK1 localizes to centrosomes. In early mitosis, it associates with mitotic spindle poles. Recombinant GFP-tagged PLK1 has been observed to localize to the centromere/kinetochore region, suggesting its involvement in chromosome separation. PLK1 is a key regulator of the G2/M transition in the cell cycle. It facilitates the functional maturation of centrosomes during late G2 and early prophase, as well as the formation of the bipolar spindle. PLK1 phosphorylates and activates CDC25C, a phosphatase that dephosphorylates and activates the cyclin B/CDK1 complex. Additionally, PLK1 phosphorylates and activates components of the anaphase-promoting complex (APC), a ubiquitin-protein ligase (E3) that degrades mitotic cyclins, chromosomal proteins maintaining sister chromatid cohesion, and anaphase inhibitors. The APC is activated by Fizzy-CDC20 family proteins. PLK1 also phosphorylates abnormal spindle (Asp), a microtubule-associated protein critical for proper spindle pole behavior and M-phase microtubule dynamics. In late mitosis, PLK1 localizes to the central spindle region and interacts with kinesin-like protein CHO1/MKLP1. In Drosophila, the homologous motor protein is encoded by the pavarotti (PAR) gene. Loss of PLK1 expression has been shown to induce pro-apoptotic pathways and inhibit cell growth. Based on studies in yeast and murine meiosis, human PLK1 may also have regulatory functions in meiosis. For example, the yeast polo kinase CDC5 is required for phosphorylating and removing meiotic cohesion during the first cell division. In CDC5-depleted cells, kinetochores are bioriented during meiosis I, and Mam1, a protein essential for coorientation, fails to associate with kinetochores. CDC5 is believed to play roles in sister-kinetochore coorientation and chromosome segregation during meiosis I. PLK1 is considered a proto-oncogene, as its overexpression is frequently observed in tumor cells. Centrosome abnormalities, particularly centrosome amplification defects, can lead to aneuploidy and tumorigenesis. PLK1 regulates centrosome duplication and maturation from late S phase to prophase. Overexpression of PLK1 increases centrosome size and/or number, resulting in improper chromosome segregation, aneuploidy, and tumorigenesis. The oncogenic properties of PLK1 are attributed to its role in driving cell cycle progression. Supporting evidence comes from studies in NIH 3T3 cells, where PLK1 overexpression enables these cells to form foci, grow in soft agar, and form tumors in nude mice. PLK1 has also been linked to pathways altered during neoplastic transformation. For instance, activation of the retinoblastoma (RB) tumor suppressor pathway represses the PLK1 promoter in a SWI/SNF chromatin remodeling complex-dependent manner. In cases of RB inactivation, PLK1 expression appears to be deregulated, suggesting that PLK1 may be a target of the RB pathway. Furthermore, PLK1 is implicated in tumor suppressor p53-related pathways. Evidence indicates that PLK1 can inhibit the transactivation and pro-apoptotic functions of p53 through physical interaction and phosphorylation. PLK1 is being actively studied as a target for cancer therapeutics. Many colon and lung cancers driven by K-RAS mutations are dependent on PLK1. Silencing PLK1 expression using RNA interference selectively kills K-RAS mutant cells without affecting normal cells. The PLK1 inhibitor volasertib is currently being evaluated in clinical trials for acute myeloid leukemia (AML). A combination of PLK1 and EGFR inhibition has been shown to overcome T790M-mediated drug resistance in vitro and in vivo in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). In head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC), mutations in AJUBA mediate sensitivity to treatment with cell-cycle inhibitors, including volasertib. Rigosertib, an experimental RAS/PI3K/PLK1 inhibitor, is also under investigation. PLK1 has been shown to interact with several proteins, including CHEK2, NUDC, PIN1, PSMA3, PSMA5, PSMA6, PSMA7, PSMB3, and TSC1. Structural analyses have provided insights into the broad specificity of PLK1.
